title: P95 econ slices & claim brief
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact working brief to unify how we talk about latency-driven unit economics (p95 slices) for sales collateral, competitive rebuttals, and benchmark asks for engineering. Goal is a reusable claim library + required proof matrix so field can make safe, verifiable statements without engineering hand-holding.

Thesis / one-liner:
Customers choose inference platforms based on predictable latency under load. By optimizing for p95 and per-request marginal cost we can claim lower end-to-end SLA cost for typical interactive workloads while offering fallbacks that preserve UX.

What we mean by "p95 econ slices":
- Slice requests into latency buckets (p50, p90, p95, p99) and show cost per successful response at each bucket for a canonical workload (chat: 512 ctx, 64 gen tokens; search: 1024 ctx embeddings).
- Focus sales language on p95 (the point most business SLAs reference) and show how batching/caching/kv-cache fallbacks reduce marginal token spend at that latency.

Primary claims (draft wording – conservative):
1) "Typical interactive apps can achieve sub-350ms p95 for short chat turns at X tokens while reducing per-response GPU token cost by 30–50% vs naive single-request serving."
2) "Redwood’s routing + prefix KV caching reduces repeat-token work by up to 4x for highway chat patterns, cutting per-session inference spend by ~40% on median usage."
3) "When capacity is constrained, our automatic fallback to quantized model variants preserves p95 SLAs while limiting per-token cost increase to <10% compared to baseline."

Important conservative language for legal/sales: always append a contextual qualifier: "based on Redwood internal benchmark X under typical interactive chat traces; results vary by prompt distribution and model size". Avoid absolute words like "always" or "guarantee" unless mapped to a paid SLA product.

Proof matrix (what we must produce to support claims):
- Workload definitions (chat short/long, assistant, retrieval-augmented), deterministic seed prompts, turn lengths.
- Test harness: distributed load generator, region-to-region latency probes, and ambient-noise scenarios.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, percentiles of cost-per-response (GPU time converted to $ using reserved capacity rates), tokens saved via cache, request-failure modes.
- Baselines: competitor public endpoints (where possible) and Redwood naive single-instance (no batching, no cache) for delta comparisons.
- Statistical confidence: 95% CI over 5 independent runs or 1M tokens processed, whichever is lower.

Benchmark plan (engineering ask):
- Run matrix: models (open-32B, 13B-quant, 7B-quant), workloads (chat-short, chat-long, rerank), concurrency sweep (1–200), regions (us-west1, eu-west1).
- Instrumentation: token-level accounting, kernel-time breakdown, queue-time, network RTT, and fallback triggers.
- Output artifacts: CSV per run, aggregated p95/cost slice charts, and a short reproducible runbook that field can cite.
- ETA ask: 3 weeks from sign-off (engineering prioritization required).

Competitive framing (unique angles):
- Comp A (public cloud ML endpoints): They publish per-token price but not p95 under load; emphasize our per-p95 cost framing as more actionable for product SLAs.
- Comp B (self-host inference runtimes): They can be cheap at bulk but require ops investment to maintain p95 under multi-tenant bursts; emphasize Redwood’s managed routing + fallbacks that capture ops cost savings.
- Comp C (vertically integrated LLM APIs): Faster on small samples but can’t show consistent p95 when customers scale; highlight our dedicated pools and verified p95 runs.

Sales one-liners and rebuttals (concise):
- Opening claim: "We measure cost per successful p95 response for your workload so you can budget reliably — not just per-token list prices."
- Rebuttal to "We can self-host cheaper": "If you factor in ops, DR, and unpredictable p95 under bursty usage, our reserved pools and autoscale policies typically reduce total monthly spend and incidents. We have customer examples and a reproducible benchmark."

Risk register & conservative mitigations:
- Risk: Benchmarks can be gamed by cherry-picked prompts. Mitigation: Publish canonical workload and seed corpus; require internal approval for public claims.
- Risk: Competitor public endpoints change behavior; Mitigation: timestamp all comparisons and keep a living table of competitor config used.
- Risk: Customer workloads differ. Mitigation: Offer a short proof-of-value (PV) test that runs customer trace through our optimizer and produces an individualized p95 econ slice.

Customer story framing (example numbers for field use — flag as "example-only"):
- Mid-market SaaS (search assistant): baseline vendor costs $0.22 per 1k tokens, p95 = 920ms at concurrency 40. Redwood PV showed p95 = 320ms and modeled monthly inference spend reduction from $17k -> $9.8k (40% lower) after enabling KV caching + moderate batching.

Required approvals & publication process:
- Engineering: confirm reproducibility and sign-off on benchmark artifacts (owner: JIRA-1428).
- Legal/Comms: approve public claim language and examples (owner: confluence page above).
- Sales enablement: write one-pager and training doc once claims validated.

Open questions for next sync:
- Which canonical customer workloads should we publish as examples? (RFPs: chat support, code-assist, search).
- Cost model assumptions for reserved capacity rates vs on-demand tokens — who finalizes? (ask finance).
- PV offering: what duration/limits do we offer for free PV runs?

Next steps (owners):
- Compile canonical workload corpus (owner: Marcus Patel) — due 2025-02-21.
- Engineering benchmark run (owner: Ravi Desai, JIRA-1428) — target 2025-03-07.
- Draft external one-pager and sales snippets (owner: Evelyn Rivera) — target 2025-03-10.

Notes to self / field tips (bullet list):
- Keep claims tied to p95 and a named workload.
- When pressed for absolute numbers, prefer "range" not single point.
- Use "per-successful-response at p95" as the canonical metric to avoid confusion with token-only unit pricing.

Finish: This is intentionally terse — the goal is a living claim bank we can iterate on after the first reproducible benchmark. Leave comments in the Confluence page and link final CSVs back to JIRA-1428.
